Demystifying AI engineering · For developers
AI changed the contract.
Software used to follow our instructions. Now it follows probabilities. That changes what engineering means.

From rules to probabilities.

Act II · The reasoning paradox
Fluent does not mean grounded.
The model predicts plausible text. Nothing in that step checks it against the facts.
Term
Token
A unit of text a model reads or writes: a word, part of a word or punctuation.
Term
Pattern matching
Using learned statistical relationships, not checking every statement.
In simple words
It knows what usually comes next, not what is true.

Act III · The reliability problem
Learning is not generating.
Two different moments in a model’s life. Two different kinds of problem.
1 · Training
The model learns patterns.
Happens once, before release. Huge datasets adjust the model’s internal weights.
Where overfitting happens
2 · Inference
The model generates an answer.
Happens every time you prompt. One token at a time, each picked from a set of options.
Where temperature applies
From rules to probabilities
08 / 26
Act III · The reliability problem
It learned the examples. Not the rule.
Like a student who memorised past exam answers: perfect on familiar questions, lost on new ones.
Term
Overfitting
The model learns its training examples too specifically, noise included, instead of generalising to unseen cases.
In simple words
Memorised the answers, not the subject.
From rules to probabilities
09 / 26
Act III · The reliability problem
How adventurous should the answer be?
Temperature reshapes the odds of the next token. It changes variety, not intelligence.
Term
Temperature
A generation setting that controls how sharply or broadly the model samples from its next-token probabilities.
In simple words
Low plays it safe. High takes a chance.

Act III · The reliability problem
Illustrative
More randomness does not mean more truth.
Temperature changes how the model picks. It doesn’t change what the model learned.
T = 0
Always the top token
// three retries
nums.sort() nums.sort() nums.sort()
→ [1, 10, 2]
Wrong: repeats the same flawed path every time
T ≈ 0.2
A little randomness
// three retries
nums.sort() nums.sort((a, b) => a - b) nums.sort((a, b) => a - b)
→ [1, 2, 10]
Right: enough room to find another route
T = 1.5
Too much randomness
// three retries
nums.sortNumeric() nums.order('asc') nums.sort(Number)
→ TypeError: not a function
Wrong: reaches for unlikely, invented tokens

Act III · The reliability problem
Sometimes, the answer is simply made up.
Missing information doesn’t stop the model. It fills the gap with something plausible.
Term
Hallucination
An AI-generated statement that sounds plausible but is incorrect, fabricated or unsupported by the available evidence.
In simple words
A confident guess dressed up as a fact.

Training
Prompt and context

Flawed data

Every answer opens more doors.
Each token opens new possible continuations. The count explodes.

A number with 470 digits
Atoms in the observable universe

Term
Combinatorial explosion
The number of possible combinations grows so fast that examining all of them becomes impractical.

Every new choice opens more doors.
Illustrative: assumes about 50,000 token choices at each step.

Act IV · The computational reality
More time unlocks more problems.
Give a computer more steps and it can provably solve problems it couldn’t before.
Linear time
Polynomial time
Exponential time
More time → strictly more solvable problems
Beyond every time limit: uncomputable
Term
Time hierarchy theorem
A result in complexity theory: with more computation time, a machine can solve problems that are impossible within a tighter time limit.
In simple words
More steps, strictly more you can solve.

The trick
Flip every circled digit. The new case differs from entry 1 in position 1, from entry 2 in position 2, and so on.
So it can’t be anywhere on the list.
Term
Diagonalization
A proof technique that constructs an example escaping a supposedly complete list or classification.
In simple words
Whatever list you make, you can build something that isn’t on it.

Act IV · The computational reality
Some problems have no general algorithm.
Not ‘too slow’. Impossible, for every possible program.
Any program
Halting checker
“Will it ever stop?”
Stops
Runs forever
The contrarian program
Asks the checker about itself, then does the opposite.
feeds itself in
If the checker says “stops”, it runs forever. The checker was wrong.
If the checker says “runs forever”, it stops. Wrong again.
No checker can be right about every program.
Term
Uncomputability
Problems for which no algorithm can give the correct answer for every possible input.
In simple words
Not too slow. Impossible in general.

Act V · The engineering trade-offs
Focus changes everything.
Attention lets each token weigh which other tokens matter for its meaning.
Term
Attention mechanism
A mechanism that lets a model weigh how relevant each input token is while processing another one.
In simple words
Listen to the words that matter.

20 / 26
Act V · The engineering trade-offs
More connections. More computation.
Every token is compared with every other token. Double the text, four times the work.
Term
Quadratic complexity
O(n²)
Computational work that grows roughly with the square of the input size.
In simple words
Twice the tokens, four times the work.
From rules to probabilities
21 / 26
Act V · The engineering trade-offs
There is a limit to what fits.
A model sees a bounded window of tokens. Older details drop out or get squeezed into summaries.
Term
Context window
How many tokens a model can take into account at once.
Term
Loss of resolution
Specific details lost when information is compressed, summarised or represented less precisely.
In simple words
Out of the window, out of mind.

22 / 26
Act V · The engineering trade-offs
The bottleneck isn’t always the engine.
For every token, the model streams its weights from memory to the processor. The road sets the pace.
Term
Memory bandwidth
The rate at which data can move between memory and the processing hardware.
In simple words
A fast factory on a narrow road.

Act VI · The realisation
We engineer around the limits.
Not just a bigger model. A better system around the model.
1 · Shape the input
Give it the right context.
Prompt engineering
Inputs that reliably get the output you need.
Context management
Focused, intent-driven context instead of everything.
2 · Right-size the model
Use specialists, not one giant.
Mixture of Experts
Route each query to a smaller, specialised expert.
Knowledge distillation
A large model teaches a smaller one.
3 · Check the output
Never ship an unchecked guess.
Guardrails
Testing & evaluation
Monitoring & iteration
Human in the loop
From uncontrolled complexity to engineered reliability.

Act VI · The realisation
Don’t engineer certainty. Engineer reliability.
AI is powerful and bounded. Our job is to understand its limits, design around them and build dependable systems within them.
